en: I am a Vice President. Nobody has ever told me of what. The desk is enormous, so I feel senior.
I have an assistant, who has an assistant. Somewhere far below me, I suspect, someone is doing my actual work.
I have a title with three words in it. I understand about one and a half of them.
People bring me papers. I move them from one side of the desk to the other. That is the whole day.
I once approved something. I still do not know what it was. Everyone seemed pleased with me.
My desk is so wide I cannot reach the far corner. That is where the real decisions must live.
When two people disagree, they bring it to me. I agree with both of them, warmly, and everyone leaves satisfied.
I have my own office and a plant. I water the plant. That part of the job I fully understand.
Every morning I put on a serious face. By noon it slides off. By evening I go looking for it.
I signed my name so many times today that I forgot how it goes. I improvised the last few.
They gave me a bigger chair last year. I do the same amount of nothing, only now much higher up.
I stand at my window and look important. From the street, I am told, I look like a small statue.
My calendar is completely full. Of what, I could not tell you. It is simply, gloriously full.
I supervise the people who do the work. They supervise themselves. I mostly supervise the coffee.
I carry a briefcase everywhere. Inside it is one apple and a spare pen. I keep the mystery alive.
When something goes wrong they send it up to me. I look at it gravely, then send it back down.
My name is on a plaque outside the door. I read it sometimes, to remember who I am meant to be.
There is a big red telephone on my desk. It has never once rung. I keep it dusted, in case importance calls.
I shook a great many hands today. I do not know whose. This counts as a productive morning.
The board asked for my opinion. I gave them a long, thoughtful pause. They wrote it down. Perfect.
I stand near the money and look serious. Nothing has ever happened. I am very good at my job.
My whole career is standing perfectly still beside a pile of money. The money moves more than I do.
The most exciting thing today was a fly. It landed on the counter. I watched it the entire time.
I have memorized every tile on this floor. There are two hundred and eleven. Ask me anything.
People think this job is thrilling. It is me, a wall, and one very locked door. For eight hours.
I practice looking alert. At home in the mirror, my wife says I look about to sneeze instead.
Nothing happens here. Then more nothing happens. Occasionally the nothing gets slightly louder.
I once caught myself asleep standing up. I called it a security patrol of my own eyelids.
My job is to be here in case something happens. In twelve years, something happened once. A dog.
I greet everyone who enters with a serious nod. They nod back. That is the whole adventure.
There is a camera watching me watch the door. Somewhere, someone watches us both. We are all extremely alert.
They trust me with a great deal of money. Mostly I am protecting it from boredom, including my own.
The alarm has never once gone off. Sometimes I imagine it going off, to keep my heart in practice.
In training they taught me to expect danger. So far the only danger is my knees, standing this long.
I stand so still that new customers ask if I am a coat rack. I let them wonder. It is more fun.
My uniform is very serious. Underneath it I am mostly thinking about lunch. Both feel important.
I watch the door. The door watches nothing. Between us, we have this entrance fully covered.
My feet know this exact spot on the floor. Two steps to the left, and my whole day feels wrong.
A child waved at me today. I gave a small wave back. My supervisor called it a lapse. I call it a highlight.
I am paid to do nothing dramatic, forever. I have exceeded every expectation. Not one dramatic thing.
People assume I must be rich, sitting beside so much money all day. I assure them the two facts are unrelated.
My hands have touched more money than most people ever see. My own wallet remains deeply unimpressed.
I slide the money across the counter and then it is gone. It is always going somewhere without me.
Every day I count to enormous numbers. Then I go home and count my own coins in about four seconds.
I know exactly how heavy a thousand coins is. Nobody has ever once asked me to demonstrate this.
People hand me their savings and I smile and give it right back. I am the least greedy person alive.
I have counted this drawer eleven times today. The number keeps agreeing with itself. Reassuring.
There is a pen chained to my counter. It has outlasted three of my coworkers. We are very close now, that pen and I.
I say the same eight sentences to every customer. By closing time they no longer sound like words.
I stamp things. I stamp so many things. If it holds still long enough, I will stamp it too.
I have a little sign that reads next window please. Sliding it into place is the most powerful thing I do all day.
I keep the money in neat, even piles. My desk at home is chaos. I ran out of neatness at work.
A person came to deposit a jar of coins. We counted them together for an hour. Best morning all week.
I hand out crisp new notes all day. They are lovely. I get to admire each one for about two seconds.
My whole job is being extremely careful with numbers that belong to strangers. I have never lost one.
I smile at everyone through a small window. By evening my face forgets how to do anything else.
I have moved the same fifty in and out of this drawer so often we are practically old friends now.
People trust me with their money the moment we meet. Nobody trusts me to pick a restaurant. Curious.
I recount whenever the total is off by one coin. Usually the coin is under my own shoe. Usually.
All day the money flows past me like a river. I am the person standing in it, staying completely dry.
I run this hotel. I have seen every kind of guest. Nothing surprises me. I practice that face daily.
A guest asked for a room with a better echo. I said of course. I have learned to just say of course.
In this job you see everything. Twice. Then a third thing arrives and quietly ruins your afternoon.
Someone requested extra pillows. Then fewer pillows. Then, thoughtfully, the exact same pillows back.
I keep a calm face no matter what walks through that door. Inside, I am often mildly astonished.
A guest complained the ocean was too loud. I nodded and wrote it down. There is nothing I can do about the ocean.
A guest asked me which direction the wind usually comes from. I gave my most confident guess. He wrote it down.
I have a smile for every situation. I have run out of situations before I have run out of smile.
A guest wanted the fourth floor moved to the second. I explained the building. He seemed let down.
My desk has a small bell. Guests ring it while looking directly at me. I still arrive, promptly, from zero distance.
Every guest believes their request is the strangest I have ever heard. They are all, somehow, correct.
I have kept this desk calm through weddings, storms, and one very determined goat. Do not ask me.
I say welcome about three hundred times a day. My face means it roughly two hundred of those times.
A guest asked if the elevator could go faster. I said I would speak to it. We had a good talk.
I have seen luggage that could not possibly fit through the door. It always fits. I stopped asking why.
The trick to this job is looking perfectly calm while, underneath the desk, both of my feet are quietly panicking.
A guest wanted a room far from the elevator, far from the stairs, and near the exit. I drew him a small diagram.
I keep the whole hotel running smoothly. The guests think it runs itself. I let them keep thinking so.
A guest told me their room was haunted. I offered a different room. It was, they reported, also haunted.
A guest asked me to name the best room. They are all the best room. I have delivered that line, calmly, for years.
I carry heavy bags to lovely rooms. The bags are not mine. The rooms are not mine. The stairs are all mine.
Today I carried a suitcase heavier than I am. Inside, the guest told me, were rocks. Only rocks.
Guests thank me and close the door. I stand in the hallway a moment, then carry my empty hands back down the stairs.
A guest packed for a weekend and brought nine bags. I did not ask. I simply carried, and I grew stronger.
I have carried every kind of bag up every kind of stair. My arms know this hotel better than I do.
People tip me for carrying things they could carry themselves. I do not complain. I am just out of breath.
I know which rooms have the good windows. I stand in them briefly, holding a stranger's coat, and I dream.
A guest asked me to carry a bag very carefully. It was empty. I carried it with great respect anyway.
My job is to move other people's things to nicer places than I will ever sleep. I do not mind. Much.
Guests hand me their bags without ever looking up. I have carried the belongings of people who never saw my face.
Someone handed me a bag and said be careful, it is fragile. Then it barked. I remain professional at all times.
I carry, I climb, I knock, I leave. Somewhere in a lovely room a bag I carried is finally resting. Lucky bag.
The heavier the bag, the longer the hallway becomes. I have measured this many times. Science keeps disagreeing.
I have opened a thousand doors for other people. I hold them, I smile, I watch others walk through. It is fine.
A guest brought a bag full of sand. For the beach, they said. The beach is outside, full of sand. I said nothing.
I carry things up. Gravity carries things down. Between us, gravity is winning, and it does no lifting at all.
My arms are the strongest part of me. My back files a formal complaint at the end of every single shift.
I have carried luggage for people going everywhere. I mostly go up four floors and then back down again.
A guest asked me to carry two heavy bags in one hand so they could film it. I obliged. My hand did not forgive me.
I set a heavy case down in a fine room, and for one moment it was my room. Then I closed the door from outside.
I solve mysteries here at the hotel. Mostly whose towels these are. It's steady work.
You chase thieves across the whole world. I once found a missing slipper. Under the bed.
I'm the detective for this one building. My whole territory ends at the parking lot.
A world detective, and then there's me. I know which guest quietly takes two breakfasts.
My biggest case this year was a lamp that walked off. It was, it turns out, in storage.
I guard the whole hotel. Four floors. Five, if you count the roof, which nobody visits.
People bring me their problems. Usually a squeaky door. I write it in my big serious notebook.
I've cracked every case in this lobby. There have been two. Both were about umbrellas.
I keep the peace across the entire hotel. My hardest days involve the ice machine.
I wear the coat, I have the badge. It says House Detective. The house is not very big.
You solve crimes on six continents. I investigate who keeps taking the good pens.
My beat is the hallway. I know every creak in it. I have named a few of the creaks.
I once tailed a suspicious guest all the way to the elevator. Then it closed. Case paused.
I'm on duty day and night. Mostly day. The night detective is a lamp at the front desk.
I investigate. I deduce. Last week I deduced the vending machine ate a coin. It had.
The hotel trusts me with its greatest secrets. So far: the pool is heated. Barely.
I keep a careful list of suspects. It is the same guest who complains about the pillows.
My office is a small room behind the desk. I've nearly solved the mystery of its smell.
I've patrolled here for years. I could find room 12 blindfolded. It's next to room 11.
Some detectives get a whole city. I got one hotel. I have investigated every square of its carpet.
I protect priceless treasures by standing here. Very still. Thinking, mostly, about lunch.
My job is to not touch the art, and to stop anyone else touching it. Mostly I stop myself.
I've stood before this painting for nine years. I still don't know what it is about.
I guard a room full of ancient gold. My chair squeaks. That is the only excitement.
People whisper in my museum out of respect. I whisper because I am half asleep.
I watch the art all day. Sometimes the art seems to watch me back. We have an understanding.
My great skill is standing perfectly still. I have been mistaken for a statue four times.
The most valuable thing here is behind glass. The second most valuable is my chair.
I protect history itself. Right now history is quiet, and I am counting the ceiling tiles.
I let nothing past this door. Not a person, not a fly. Especially not a fly. Flies keep me busy.
I stand guard from morning to night. The paintings never leave. Neither, it seems, do I.
Someone asked what I do all day. I stand here and watch, I said. They called it boring. Accurate.
I've memorized every crack in this old floor. It's a hobby now. It's the only hobby.
My uniform says security. My feet say sit down. We argue about this all day.
I guard treasures worth more than my whole town. And I am thinking about a sandwich.
There is an alarm for emergencies. In fifteen years it has rung twice. Both times, my elbow.
The rule is simple: don't let anyone take the art. So far, wonderfully, nobody has tried.
I watch a golden vase all day. It does nothing. I do nothing. We are a good team.
Visitors think this job is glamorous. Then they see me stretching my back very slowly.
I could name every painting here with my eyes closed. Some days I do, to pass the time.
I point at old things and explain why they matter. People nod. I love the nodding.
My job is to make a very old pot sound thrilling. Some days I even believe it myself.
I give the tour twelve times a day. By noon I could give it asleep. Sometimes I do.
I stop at each object and say something meaningful. The objects have heard it all before.
I lead groups through the museum. My whole skill is walking slowly and pointing well.
I explained a chair for ten minutes today. A very old, very important chair. Nobody sat.
I say 'and if you look here' about forty times a day. My finger is the hardest worker.
People come to learn. I come to point at things. Together we make a lovely afternoon.
My tour has a big finish. It is a small vase. I've learned to build the suspense anyway.
I know a hundred stories about these objects. The objects have never once thanked me.
On today's tour a small boy asked if the statue was alive. I said no. He wasn't convinced. Fair.
I walk backwards while I talk so I can face the group. I have not fallen yet. Yet.
I describe every brushstroke of a painting. It takes twenty minutes. The painting waits.
My greatest tool is my pointing hand. My second is knowing when to stop pointing.
I lead people from room to room, explaining. It's just slow, very well-informed walking.
I've given this tour so often the objects feel like coworkers. Quiet coworkers. Old ones.
I make history come alive. Mostly by talking about it until someone's stomach growls.
The tour ends exactly where it began. A tidy loop. My feet have filed a complaint about the loop.
I point at a thousand-year-old jar and everyone gasps. I did the gasp first, years ago.
My job is enthusiasm about the past. It's easier before lunch. The past waits patiently.
I know the story of every object here. Long stories. I tell them at parties. Invitations are rare.
I can tell you where each piece came from and how old it is. My own age I keep politely vague.
Forty years I have cared for this collection. It has never been smaller than it is right now.
I know these objects like family. And like family, one of them has quietly slipped out.
Ask me anything about this collection. Anything at all. Just not about that empty shelf.
I chose every object here myself. I did not choose for one of them to go for a walk.
I've catalogued each piece down to the smallest scratch. My own handwriting is the true mystery.
My whole life is knowing where things belong. A spot on the wall now firmly disagrees.
I could recite this collection from memory. I'll skip one item, for reasons we won't discuss.
Every object here has a story. One of them, it turns out, has an ending I didn't write.
I labeled every case in this building. One label now describes a very tidy empty box.
I know the age of every treasure here to the year. And the exact minute one of them left.
People call me the keeper of the collection. Today I kept most of it. Most is a strong word.
I've dusted these shelves for decades. There is one shelf now that dusts unusually fast.
I remember when each piece arrived. Some came by ship, some by truck, one in a sad little envelope.
I wrote the book on this collection. I may need to add a short, sad new chapter.
I can find any object here with my eyes shut. My glasses, however, defeat me every single morning.
The collection is my life's work. Today my life's work has a small, cool breeze through it.
I know every piece so well I could draw them. My drawings resemble potatoes. Very old potatoes.
A child asked where the golden mask went. I, the expert, said the one thing experts dread: hm.
I serve food all day. Kings and rascals, same manners, same complaint: too slow.
Everyone at every table wants their meal faster. I have not yet learned to walk through walls.
I've served the rich and the rude. They order differently. They complain identically.
My job is carrying plates and smiling. The plates are heavy. The smiling is heavier.
A very important guest sent back the soup. It was, he said, too warm. It is soup.
I remember every order but never my own dinner, which I eat standing up at midnight.
I've balanced eleven plates on two arms. Nobody claps. They just ask for more bread.
Kings, thieves, everyone leaves the same tip. Which is to say, we don't talk about tips.
I carry hot food across a crowded room without spilling. It is my one great talent. Truly.
Someone ordered the chef's finest dish, then removed half the ingredients. Same as ever.
I hear every complaint in the world at these tables. My reply is always the same warm nod.
I've served people who own castles. They still ask if the water is free. It is.
My feet have walked a hundred miles between the kitchen and table four. Table four is fussy.
A grand guest snapped his fingers at me. I came. That is the job. The fingers, though.
Everyone wants the window seat. I do not control the windows. I've explained this often.
I refill water glasses all evening. Fill, empty, fill. It is the tide, but indoors.
One guest ordered the costly dish, then asked why it was so small. It is costly because it is small.
I've memorized the whole menu. Guests still ask what is good. Everything. It's all good.
I smile at every table, even the loud one. Especially the loud one. That is the real work.
I bring the food, I take the plates, I never sit. My chair at home barely knows me.
I'm paid to teach forehands. Mostly I nod while people tell me about their week.
Today's lesson was one serve and forty minutes of talking about a fence.
I get more exercise fetching balls than my students get from hitting them.
Nobody comes here to learn tennis. They come to be listened to, near a net.
The ball machine never argues about the score. It is my favorite student.
We warm up for ten minutes and play for two. Stretching is the whole sport now.
I fix their grip, they thank me warmly, then hold it exactly as wrong as before.
Two hours on the court today. I hit maybe four balls. Heard about four hundred things.
We take a water break every four minutes. Hydration has become the real workout.
I could teach a wall. The wall would at least stay on its side of the net.
I run to every corner of the court so my students can stand still and watch.
They pay me to improve their game, then spend the whole hour explaining why today doesn't count.
I keep score for people who stopped playing twenty minutes ago.
My best students are the ones who occasionally remember there's a ball.
I demonstrate a perfect swing. Nobody watches. Everybody claps anyway.
New racket, new shoes, a matching outfit. The actual swing arrives whenever it feels ready.
I used to say 'bend your knees.' The knees and I have quietly agreed to stop.
Some days I'm a coach. Most days I'm a friend who happens to own a net.
They dress for a championship, then spend an hour hunting for the ball in a bush.
I supply the balls, the rackets, and the encouragement. Mostly they misplace the balls.
People tell me their deepest secrets. By closing time I've forgotten every one.
People ask me for advice. I offer a napkin and a glass of water. Same result, honestly.
Everyone assumes I remember them. I remember the drink. Never the story.
One man has ordered the exact same drink for years. I deeply admire the commitment.
Someone returned a drink for having one too few olives. I added three. Peace was restored.
A man told me his whole life last night. I nodded. I retained the ice request.
People think I'm wise. I'm just standing still while they talk.
I know everything about everyone here, for exactly the length of one glass.
At the end of the night I call last orders, and everyone suddenly has much more to say.
My memory holds two things: the specials, and absolutely none of your secrets.
I've been told forty personal crises this week. Ask me one. I dare you.
The tip jar and I have the same job tonight: sitting here, looking hopeful, staying almost empty.
A customer wanted water, but fancier. I served it in a nicer glass. They were delighted.
Someone told me a huge secret an hour ago. It was, I'm sure, a very good one.
The bar is the safest place in town. I couldn't testify to anything.
I remember every order. I forget every heartbreak. It's a useful arrangement.
I wipe the same glass clean forty times a night. It gives my hands something to do.
My hardest task is telling a very happy person that they have had quite enough happiness.
A regular tells me the same long story every week. I have started to enjoy the ending.
I've recited today's specials three hundred times. By now I believe in them completely.
I check books out, I check books in. The excitement rarely peaks in between.
All day I move books six inches to the left, then back again.
My job is a book comes, a book goes. I am the small door it passes through.
I set the date stamp each morning. It is the single most powerful decision of my day.
The most dramatic thing here is a book returned one day late.
I've handled ten thousand books today and read the spine of none of them.
Books come to me full of stories. I only ever check the little card.
It is very quiet work. My biggest decision is which stamp needs more ink.
Books drop through the return slot all night. I like to imagine they had adventures.
A visitor owed a fine of two coins today. We discussed it as though it were a fortune.
A book goes out. A week later it returns. This is my entire tide.
I know where every book lives. I've simply never opened one to find out why.
The days are calm. A cart with a squeaky wheel is a genuine event.
The hold shelf is where books wait for people who requested them and then vanished forever.
Someone renewed the same book all year. Neither of us truly believes they will read it.
I've perfected the quiet slide of a book across a desk. It took years.
I stack the return cart very neatly. Nobody has ever noticed. I keep doing it anyway.
I own a stamp, a pencil, and a very small bell. A wild day is when I get to use all three.
I issued a new library card today. Briefly, I felt like I was handing over a great privilege.
By closing I have spoken perhaps nine words, four of them concerning a stapler.
I spend half my day whispering 'quiet' and the other half knowing everything.
People approach my desk of near-infinite knowledge to ask where the printer is.
The reading room is meant for deep research. Mostly it hosts very dignified naps.
I give people the precisely correct answer. Half of them decide to disagree with it anyway.
A visitor once asked a question I actually had to look up. It was the finest moment of my year.
I once answered a question so obscure I surprised myself. Then I shushed a cough.
I sit at a desk built for the hardest questions. Today's hardest was what the date is.
I dust encyclopedias last opened before I was born. Over the years, we have grown close.
Someone asked one small question. I delivered the entire history. They slowly backed away.
People are amazed I know so much. I'm amazed anyone here can hear me at all.
I answer questions all day at a volume slightly below a passing cloud.
I can find any book from memory. The catalog and I compete politely, and I am winning.
Some days a single person visits my desk. I treat their question as a royal audience.
I hold a great many facts, and I frown, very quietly, at loud shoes.
I once corrected a footnote that no one will ever read. It remains my proudest achievement.
I could win any argument. I would simply do it too quietly for anyone to notice.
People forget I'm here until they need a fact. Then I appear, softly, with three.
I hush the room, then answer a stranger's question about the entire universe.
The louder the question, the quieter I answer. It's a small act of protest.
People whisper their questions to me as if the books nearby might overhear and grow jealous.
I can tell you anything about two hundred years ago. Today, I'm completely lost.
I file the past into tiny boxes. The present keeps refusing to fit in one.
I'm an expert on a century I never lived in and a stranger to this one.
Ask me about the year 1820. Ask me about this morning and I go quite still.
I wear soft gloves to handle things older than most nations. Then I go home and drop a plate.
I read handwriting from long before you were born. My own notes defeat me by lunchtime.
I've spent decades organizing the past. It's the only era I feel at home in.
I can date a letter to the exact decade. I could not tell you today's date.
The past is neatly labeled and boxed. The present is out there, unsorted, loud.
I keep two hundred years in careful order and my own week in total chaos.
People come to me for history. Nobody comes to me for the news, and rightly so.
I keep the room colder than anyone likes, so the paper can outlive us all in comfort.
Three people visited the archive this year. Each of them I now consider a close friend.
My expertise stops precisely at the moment I was born, and it has learned nothing since.
I know what happened in a distant year better than what happened at breakfast.
Everything here smells faintly of two centuries ago. I stopped noticing. Guests never do.
I preserve the old world beautifully. The new one keeps arriving without labels.
I can find a letter from long ago in seconds. My keys, however, are gone forever.
No food, no drink, no sudden movements near the documents. The past bruises very easily.
Some pages would crumble at a sneeze. So I have learned, professionally, never to sneeze.
I fly to places all day. I have never once been asked to stay and look around.
The passengers all know where they're going. I just point the plane and hope they agree.
I have landed in more cities than I can name. I saw the runway of each one, briefly.
People thank me for a smooth flight. I nod, as if smoothness was my decision and not luck.
I've flown over every mountain worth flying over. From up here they all look like wrinkles.
My whole job is to leave. I have gotten very good at leaving. Staying, less so.
I announce the weather like I checked it myself. I did not. A screen told me.
I've seen a thousand sunrises from the sky. I would trade some for one full night of sleep.
Everyone claps when we land. I appreciate it. Landing is, in fairness, the important part.
I know the sky better than my own street. My own street keeps moving the parking.
I fly for a living, and yet I still get nervous when someone else drives to the airport.
The best part of the job is the view. The second best is that no one can hand me their bags.
I have flown for years. I still cannot tell you what the little dial on the left actually does.
I take people to their reunions, meetings, and beaches. I go back to the airport.
My office has the finest view in the world, and no place at all to hang a picture.
I've circled the same tower forty times waiting to land. We became close, that tower and I.
I carry hundreds of people and remember none. They carry snacks and remember everything.
People ask if I ever get bored up there. Only when nothing is trying to go wrong.
I spend my days above the clouds. It is lovely, and it is also just a very high desk.
I have a hat, a schedule, and absolutely no idea what my passengers packed.
I have met every type of person alive. In the end, they all want a second bag of pretzels.
I walk more in one flight than most people walk in a week, all in a very narrow hallway.
I've calmed nervous flyers, crying babies, and grown adults who wanted the shade just so.
People treat the cart like a surprise. It comes every flight. It has never once not come.
I demonstrate the seatbelt with great care. Everyone watches the one thing they already know.
I've handed out thousands of cups of water. People take one sip, then hand it right back to me.
I ask 'chicken or pasta' so often I dream it. The dream has no correct answer either.
I remember faces for exactly one flight. Then they land and become someone else's problem, kindly.
My smile is professional and my feet are honest. Only one of them survives the whole trip.
People ask where we are. I tell them the sky. They wanted more detail. So did I, once.
First-time flyers grip the armrest. Thousandth-time flyers grip it too, only with more practiced calm.
I point at the exits with two flat hands. It is the calmest I look all day, and it is a lie.
Someone always presses the button the moment I sit down. I no longer fight it. The button wins.
I collect the little cups afterward. So many little cups. A quiet parade of little cups.
I've comforted people afraid of turbulence by pretending I have never once thought about it.
The job is mostly kindness and balance, delivered sideways, while carrying something hot.
I know every word on the safety card. I have watched exactly no one else read a single one.
People board tired and leave tired. In between, they mostly want a blanket and a snack.
I have said 'welcome aboard' more times than my own name. I answer to both now.
My cart is small, the aisle is smaller, and somehow everyone's elbow still finds it.
I send bags all over the world. Some of them see more of it than their owners do.
A suitcase left this morning. It will arrive somewhere. We are both hopeful about where.
I have lifted every kind of bag. The heavy ones are always labeled 'fragile, this way up.'
People trust me with everything they packed. I trust the belt, and the belt is doing its best.
Some bags travel farther than I ever will. I wave them off like a proud, tired luggage parent.
I match every bag to a tag. Now and then a bag decides it would rather go on holiday alone.
I learn a lot about people from their suitcases. Mostly that they packed too many shoes.
A bag went one way and its owner the other. They will be reunited. Probably. Eventually.
I have seen a suitcase held together with one hopeful strap and a great deal of optimism.
My job is to keep bags in order. The bags have their own ideas about order.
Every day I move a small city's worth of belongings, and none of them thank me.
People ask if their bag will make it. I say yes with the calm of a man who is only mostly sure.
I've handled a suitcase heavier than me. It won. I filed the paperwork from the floor.
A bag once traveled to three places before its owner. It came back with no stories to share.
I read the tags all day. It is like reading everyone's travel plans without any of the fun.
The belt goes round and round. Sometimes a lonely bag rides it for hours, seeing the sights.
I return lost bags to grateful people. The bags say nothing. The bags never say anything.
Some luggage arrives before its owner and just waits there, quietly pleased with itself.
I have grown fond of one green suitcase. It travels the world constantly. I have never once left this room.
My whole day is other people's things going elsewhere. I stay by the belt, and the belt stays with me.
I have sailed to the far corners of the world. I remember them as wet, and quite far away.
People ask about the exotic places I've seen. I mostly saw the same six seabirds, hoping for scraps.
I've crossed more seas than I can count. On each, something slid off the table, and I let it go.
I've been everywhere by boat. The ocean, I have learned, has no signs telling you which part you are in.
The sea has taken me to distant shores. I mostly recall the sea, and a strong wish for dry socks.
I've sailed for decades. My memories are a blur of horizon, salt, and one very good soup.
People think a sailor's life is romantic. It is mostly rope, weather, and looking at more water.
I have seen sights no landlocked soul has seen. I described them once as blue, then more blue.
I could navigate by the stars. Lately I navigate by whoever seems most confident on deck.
Every port looks different and every sea looks the same. I have accepted the sea's routine.
I've sailed the whole globe. People ask about the sunsets. After enough of them, I mostly just check if it is bedtime.
The waves rock me to sleep every night. On land, the floor refuses to do its part.
I've weathered great storms. I remember them the way one remembers a bad meeting: loudly, and wetly.
Ask me the best place I've sailed to and I will think, then describe the harbor with the emptiest dock.
I know a hundred knots and I use the same three. The other ninety-seven are for showing off.
The horizon is my whole view. It never gets closer. We have an understanding, the horizon and I.
I've spent so long at sea that a puddle now feels like coming home.
People want tales of high adventure. My best one is about a very large wave I mostly slept through.
I've dropped anchor in more harbors than I can name, which is handy, as I can name none.
The sea is my whole career and I still could not tell you what is at the bottom of it.
I run the harbor. I do not leave the harbor. I still, somehow, manage to get seasick.
Every boat here answers to me. The seagulls answer to no one, and they are quite smug about it.
I've stood at this dock for years. I can recite the tide's schedule, but never remember my own lunch.
I direct ships in and out all day. The one place I never go is out.
The sailors sail off to adventure. I stay behind and fill out a small form for every one that leaves.
I know every vessel in this harbor by name. I have set foot on precisely none of them.
People assume a harbor master loves the sea. I love it deeply, from a firm and unmoving distance.
I keep order among a hundred boats. Order among a hundred boats is a generous word for it.
My whole world is this one patch of water and its comings and goings. The comings, mostly.
I watch the tides all day. They come, they go, they never once ask my opinion.
I have the finest view of the water, and I spend most of the day looking down at a clipboard instead.
Ships arrive with grand stories. I nod, wave them to a berth, and return to my very still chair.
I signal the boats where to go. Where I go is the same office, every day, at the same slow pace.
The harbor never sleeps, which is a kind way of saying neither, most nights, do I.
I am in charge of everything that floats here. I, personally, would rather not float at all.
Every captain thinks their arrival is special. To me it is one more day, with a bit more rope involved.
People ask me the fastest way to the sea. I point straight ahead. It is always, reliably, straight ahead.
My desk faces the water. The water faces me back. Between us we have solved nothing.
I count the boats in, I count the boats out. The numbers should match. It's a good day when they do.
I stay firmly on land while everyone drifts off. Someone has to be here when they all drift back in.
I ask everyone the same question all day: anything to declare? Almost everyone says no. Almost everyone is wrong.
My whole job is one question. You would think people would practice the answer before they reach my desk.
Someone once said no, then remembered a live turtle in their coat. We both took a quiet moment.
People forget the strangest things. A whole cheese. A second suitcase. Once, a small tree.
I ask what you are carrying. The honest ones list three things. The bag, if asked, would list nine.
A man told me he had nothing to declare, then his bag began to hum. I still think about that bag.
I have heard every version of nothing. Some of them weigh forty pounds.
My favorite moment is when a perfectly calm face suddenly remembers the one thing it hoped I would not ask about.
You declare nothing. I nod. Then I open the bag and we both learn something new.
I spend my days sorting the honest travelers from the optimistic ones. Usually they turn out to be the same traveler.
People pack their whole life into a bag, then swear the bag is empty. I admire the confidence.
Anything to declare, I ask. They pause. That pause tells me more than any answer ever could.
Once a traveler declared a sandwich. Just one sandwich. Honestly, it was refreshing.
The job is simple: ask, wait, believe nothing, and smile the whole time anyway.
I have watched grown adults forget an entire second coat they were, at that moment, wearing.
Every day I learn what people think does not count. It is usually the biggest item in the bag.
A woman said no, then produced eleven jars of jam from a coat clearly designed for holding jam.
I ask, they answer, and somewhere at their feet a suitcase quietly disagrees with all of it.
This job trained me to notice the one bag a person is trying very hard not to look at.
People declare the boring things and forget the interesting ones. To be fair, so would I.
I lift boxes all day. I do not know what is inside them. I stopped wondering a long time ago.
My back has opinions now. It shares them every morning, loudly, before I have even stood up.
I carried a crate today that weighed more than I do. We did not part as friends.
People ask what I do. I move heavy things from one place to a slightly less convenient place.
Every crate looks the same until you lift it. Then it becomes a very personal experience.
Once a huge crate turned out to be completely empty. I have never felt more personally betrayed by a box.
The dock has one rule: if it is heavy, it belongs to me. Everything here is heavy.
I moved forty crates before lunch. Then lunch arrived, and it was also heavy, so I moved that too.
You grow strong doing this. You also grow very good at not thinking about your knees.
A crate today was marked fragile. It weighed as much as a small horse. I was gentle anyway.
My whole life is picking up one heavy thing and setting it down near another heavy thing.
I do not ask what is in the boxes. Curiosity has never once helped me lift one.
Some days the crates win. You set them down, nod at them, and agree to try again tomorrow.
I have strong arms and a short memory. Both are absolutely required for this job.
The heaviest crate always sits at the very bottom. I suspect the dock was designed by someone who dislikes me.
I stacked boxes taller than my own house. Then someone told me they go on a different boat.
People think it is all muscle. It is mostly patience, and a little quiet complaining under my breath.
I carried something so heavy today that I briefly forgot my own name. It was a peaceful moment.
The crates never say thank you. Years ago, I stopped waiting for them to start.
Lift it, carry it, set it down, do it again. My shoulders keep a very detailed record of every single one.
My boat is small. The ships are enormous. Somehow I am in charge, and it surprises me daily.
I push things a hundred times my size. My little boat has never once complained. I complain plenty.
People see a giant ship move and assume it decided to. No. That was me, and my very small boat.
The ship weighs more than a mountain. I nudge it politely and hope very much for the best.
My entire career is convincing enormous things to move slightly to the left.
I have the smallest boat in the harbor and the largest responsibilities in it. It works, mostly.
A ship this big has no idea where the harbor entrance is. Luckily, one very small boat knows exactly.
I spend my days pushing something that could crush me, very slowly, and with great affection.
A ship this size cannot stop quickly. So mostly my job is starting to stop it long before anyone thinks we should.
Push too hard and the ship swings the wrong way. So I push almost gently, and apologize quietly when I do not.
People wave at the giant ship. Nobody waves at the little boat doing all the work. I wave back anyway.
My boat is tiny and stubborn. Between the two of us, the stubborn part does most of the actual work.
I once pushed a ship so long that by the time the front reached the dock, the back was still thinking about it.
The trick is patience. You cannot rush something that big. Believe me, over the years I have tried.
My job is being small and confident next to something huge and helpless. We truly need each other.
I spend hours moving a ship a short distance. It is the most important short distance in the harbor.
A giant vessel, a tiny boat, and me in the middle, quietly steering the whole disagreement.
People underestimate small boats. So do the big ships, right up until the moment I push them.
I do not fight the big ships. I lean on them, gently, until they finally agree to go where I want.
My boat is little. My determination is not. That, honestly, is the entire job.
I know four phrases. I use all four constantly. It has served me beautifully so far.
I heard something. I will now repeat it to everyone, forever. This is my job. I adore my job.
I want a cracker. I wanted one before you arrived. I will want one long after you leave.
I sit on a shoulder and repeat what people say. Nobody tells me secrets anymore. I cannot imagine why.
I have strong opinions and one tiny beak. Both of them are extremely loud.
The sailors lower their voices whenever I am near. It never helps. My hearing is the best thing about me.
I only know a few words, but I say each one at maximum volume. Also, I would like a cracker.
People think I do not understand them. I understand plenty. I simply choose to shout it back.
I repeat the gossip whether or not it is true. Accuracy was never part of my job description.
I have sat on this shoulder for years. I have heard everything. I have kept none of it to myself.
Give me a cracker and I will tell you nothing useful, loudly, and with tremendous confidence.
I know exactly three things, and I am wrong about one of them. I will not tell you which.
The captain keeps telling me to be quiet. The captain does not seem to know who is truly in charge here.
I repeat what I hear. If you did not want it repeated, you should not have said it near a bird.
I have opinions about the weather, the food, and you specifically. Mostly about the cracker situation.
Everyone thinks the parrot is decoration. The parrot heard what you said last night. The parrot remembers.
I say the same phrase a hundred times a day. It is a good phrase. Why change something that works.
I would tell you a secret, but first, and this part is important, I am going to need a cracker.
I am small, I am loud, and I know things. It is a dangerous combination, and I enjoy every part of it.
They taught me polite words. I use them to spread gossip. On the whole, a very fair trade.
I am not allowed to move a single muscle. The pigeons figured this out weeks ago. They now treat me as furniture.
Standing perfectly still is the entire job. You would be amazed how tiring doing nothing can be.
I have stood here for hours without moving. My greatest enemy today is one very persistent itch.
Visitors pose beside me for photos. I hold the pose far better than they do. It is the one contest I always win.
My job is to be a statue that quietly breathes. Most days I forget the breathing part is even allowed.
I may not move. I may not speak. Yet here I am, doing both, for you. Please do not tell anyone.
People try to make me laugh all day. They fail. But I keep a small private list of the good ones.
My greatest professional skill is looking like a man who is not counting the minutes. I am always counting the minutes.
The rule is no blinking. I blink. I am, in my own small way, a rebel. Please keep this between us.
I stand guard for hours and nothing happens. I guard that nothing with tremendous dedication.
Small children salute me all day long. I am not permitted to salute back. That, honestly, is the hardest rule of all.
My whole training was learning to do absolutely nothing, flawlessly, for a very long time.
A fly landed on my nose this morning. I did not move. That was the highlight of my entire week.
I am not supposed to react to anything. So whatever you do, I will stand here and quietly judge it.
The uniform is warm and the pose never changes. On long afternoons I am fairly sure I nap standing up, unnoticed.
Guides walk past and describe me to strangers as if I cannot hear. I hear all of it. I remember the flattering parts.
I stand so still that visitors check whether I am real. I let them wonder. It helps pass the time.
My back aches, my feet ache, and I am allowed to show none of it. Being a statue has hidden costs.
I am risking a great deal to tell you this: it is very, very boring being this impressive.
They chose me to stand here because I never fidget. If they only knew what my mind does all day.
My job is to stand very still and look serious. I am extremely good at both.
I was told to guard this spot. Nobody said until when, so I assume forever.
I follow orders. Today's order was 'wait here.' I have been winning at it all day.
I stood so still a bird sat on my helmet. I let it stay. It seemed to have a plan.
Guarding is mostly standing. Standing is mostly thinking about sitting.
I've been at this post so long I've given all the cracks in the wall names.
They gave me a spear and a place to stand. The spear does less than you would think.
My commander says patience is a weapon. If so, I am dangerously well armed.
I waited four hours for an order. The order was to keep waiting. I respect the consistency.
I salute, I stand, I wait. Then, for variety, I stand a little differently.
I guarded this gate all morning. A cat walked through. I let it. It outranks me in confidence.
Following orders is simple. The hard part is remembering which way I was told to face.
I stand watch so nothing happens. So far, a triumph. Nothing keeps not happening.
My feet fell asleep at this post. I did not. Someone has to stay alert.
I've stared down this road so long I feel like I own it. I do not own it.
They spent a year training me to march. I have spent every year since standing perfectly still.
Waiting is my whole trade. I have gotten so good I can do it with my eyes half open.
A soldier waits. I have waited for orders, for weather, for lunch, and now for this chat.
I hold this position no matter what. Nobody has tested it, but I stay ready and slightly bored.
I stand guard through rain and sun. Mostly I stand guard through nothing at all.
I lean in close and whisper wisdom. Most of it is 'perhaps we should wait and see.'
I advise the crown on grave matters. This morning the grave matter was the breakfast menu.
I say things slowly and importantly. It makes the smallest suggestion sound enormous.
My advice is always the same: proceed with caution. I have built a whole career on it.
I whisper into royal ears. Half of what I whisper is simply 'that is a wise question.'
A councillor must look thoughtful at all times. I furrow my brow even when I am only hungry.
I gave a long, grand speech today. Its point was that we should think about it a while longer.
I nod gravely, stroke my chin, and say 'indeed.' That is roughly ninety percent of the job.
They pay me to have opinions. I have learned to have them very, very slowly.
My counsel is priceless. It is also, if I am honest, mostly 'let us not be hasty.'
I stand near the throne and murmur. The murmuring is the important part, apparently.
I advised the king to wait until morning before deciding. It is my finest and most frequent advice.
I speak in a low, wise voice. Even 'good morning' sounds like a warning when I say it.
Grand titles, grand robes, grand whispers. The whispers usually mean 'ask someone else.'
I am consulted on everything. My answer to everything is a long, meaningful pause.
A councillor never rushes. I have kept the whole court waiting on a single word for an hour.
I whisper my advice so no one can steal it. Mostly no one else wants it.
I bow deeply and speak wisely. The wisdom, this time, is that we should form a committee.
I have advised three kings. Each one, in the end, did the opposite. I remain very proud.
My whole role is to look wise and lean in close. The leaning is surprisingly tiring.
I watch numbers go up and down all day. Today they went down, then up, then it was lunch.
My job is to stare at the numbers until they mean something. I am patient. The numbers are more patient.
The numbers rose. Then they fell. I wrote down that they did both. That is the whole report.
I study patterns for a living. Today's pattern was that I got hungry at exactly the same time.
A number went up. I felt joy. It came back down. I felt informed.
I watch the figures so closely that when they blink, I blink too. They do not blink.
My conclusion, after hours of careful study, is that the numbers are up. Also that they are down.
I turn columns of numbers into meaning. Today the meaning was 'perhaps have a sandwich.'
The chart went up sharply. My heart went with it. Then the chart quietly changed its mind.
I have looked at these numbers so long I have started to root for a few of them.
People ask me what the numbers mean. I tell them, gravely, 'it depends.' They nod as if satisfied.
I predicted the numbers would move. They moved. I have never been so unsurprised.
My whole trade is watching things rise and fall. Today, mostly, it was my own attention.
The figures wobbled all morning. I wrote 'the figures wobbled.' It is a strong report.
I sat with these numbers until they confessed. They confessed nothing. They are a very disciplined bunch.
I measure everything. This morning I measured how long until I could reasonably stop measuring.
The numbers are telling a story. It is a slow story. It is mostly about the numbers.
I found meaning in the data at last. It was a very small meaning. I wrote it down anyway.
Up, down, up again. I nod at each one as if I expected it. I did not.
My job is patience and columns. Today the columns won, and my patience quietly left for lunch.
I shout 'buy' and 'sell' all day. Now I shout them at home too, at the soup.
My reflexes are stuck from the trading floor. I nearly bought a passing pigeon this morning.
I've spent so long yelling numbers that I greeted my own mother with a price.
Buy, sell, buy, sell. I do it so fast I sometimes sell things I quite liked.
The floor is loud. I am loud. When I go quiet, people ask if something is wrong.
I raised my hand to wave hello and accidentally agreed to a very large deal.
My hands move faster than my thoughts. Some days I trade before I have fully woken up.
I shout all day at the exchange. My voice has two settings now: loud and slightly less loud.
I sold, then bought, then sold again, all before breakfast. Breakfast was not for sale.
My reflexes never switch off. I flinched at a falling leaf as if it were terrible news.
I buy high, sell higher, and shout the whole time. My throat files a complaint every evening.
On the floor I never stop moving. At dinner my hand still signals for prices no one is offering.
I've shouted 'sold' so often that I once said it when a waiter cleared my plate.
Fast hands, loud voice, quick decisions. Choosing what to have for lunch, though, takes me an hour.
I trade all day at full speed. When I finally sit still, the whole room feels too slow.
Somebody sneezed and my hand shot up to make an offer. Old habits are very fast habits.
I yell buy, I yell sell, I yell it with my whole chest. Quiet rooms make me deeply nervous.
My reflexes are so trained that I once made a bid at my own reflection. It did not accept.
All day it is prices and shouting. By evening I can only whisper, and I still whisper numbers.
I make a hundred snap decisions before noon. Then I cannot decide which chair to sit in.
I run notes across the whole city on foot. I have met every hill in it, personally.
I have the fastest legs in town and, by a wide margin, the sorest feet.
I ran three notes across the city before noon. Then I looked around for a fourth, out of pure habit.
My job is to run and not read. I have carried a thousand secrets, and kept every one unread.
I know every street, every shortcut, every stray dog by name. The dogs, sadly, do not know mine.
I delivered a note so fast the sender was still writing the next one when I got back.
People say I fly across town. I do not. I run. My feet would like this clearly noted.
I've run this city end to end so often I could do it with my eyes closed. I have not tried.
My legs never tire. My feet, however, hold a grudge that grows a little bigger each day.
I carry messages, not opinions. I once delivered an insult and a love note in one trip, at the same speed.
I once raced a rider on a horse across town. I lost. But I looked far more determined about it.
I have a perfect memory for doorways and none for faces. I reach the right house and greet the wrong person.
I run all day and rest by walking slowly. My idea of a relaxing holiday is a gentle jog.
I've worn out more shoes than I can count. The shoes gave up. My legs did not.
I delivered forty notes today. I remember every single route and not one single word.
They call me the fastest in the city. I have never slowed down enough to see if it is true.
I run so much that when I finally sit down, my legs keep going without me for a moment.
I've crossed this city so many times I recognize the cobblestones one by one.
My whole trade is speed. I am so used to hurrying that now I eat, sleep, and think quickly too.
I carried an urgent note across town in record time. It said 'no reply needed.' They always do.
I sell hats. Just hats. If you want gossip, that stall is two down and much cheaper.
I shout about hats all day. My voice is tired. The hats are fine.
People ask if the hats come with a story. No. They come with a brim.
I have forty hats and one customer. He is looking at the trinkets.
A good hawker sells you a hat you did not know you wanted. I am a good hawker.
I called out to a hundred people today. Two waved. One bought a hat.
My trinkets are shiny. My hats are practical. I recommend both, loudly.
I know every face on this street. I do not know their names. I know their hat size.
Someone asked me for a secret. I offered a hat instead. He took the hat.
I sell hats, not information. The hats are much better made.
By evening I have no voice left, so I sell the last few hats by pointing and looking hopeful.
I can spot a head that needs a hat from across the square. It is a quiet talent.
A trinket for luck, a hat for the sun. I do not sell luck, honestly.
I lowered my voice once, to rest it. Sold nothing. Back to shouting.
The best hat I own is on my own head. It is not for sale. Do not ask.
Children like the trinkets. Adults pretend not to. Then they buy two.
I have described this hat forty times today. It is still just a hat.
My stall is loud on purpose. A quiet hat seller is just a man standing near hats.
I do not pick my customers. The sun does. On a bright day, everyone suddenly needs a hat.
End of the day, I count the hats I have left. That tells me how loud to be tomorrow.
I could sell this at the asking price. But then what would we talk about?
Every coin matters to me. I once haggled over one for a full hour. I enjoyed it.
You offer half, I ask for double, we meet in the middle. That is friendship.
I do not lose sleep over the goods. I lose sleep over the last coin of a good haggle.
A customer paid my full price today without arguing. I felt cheated, somehow.
A quick sale leaves me restless. Make me fight for every coin, or I feel we skipped the good part.
My prices are firm. My prices are also flexible. It depends on how you ask.
I count my coins twice each night. Once for the total, once for the joy of it.
Everything on this stall has two prices. The one I say, and the one you earn.
You want a discount? Sit down. This will take a while, and I have tea.
I have argued over the price of a button. I regret nothing. I won the button.
A fair deal is one where we both walk away sure we cheated the other.
I never name my lowest price first. That would end the conversation too soon.
Some sell to be rich. I sell to argue. The coins are just how we keep score.
You will pay more than you wanted and less than I hoped. That is a good market.
I remember every haggle I have ever lost. There are two. I still think about them.
My grandmother taught me to haggle. She once argued with the tax man, and won.
The goods change every week. The bargaining does not. That is the real business.
I raised my price when you frowned, because a frown means you still want it.
Come back tomorrow and we will do this all again. I look forward to it, truly.
Grown-ups walk right past me. So I see everything they do when they think no one is.
Nobody watches a kid. That is why a kid sees the most. Also, do you have any bread?
I know which stalls watch me closely and which do not. I remember the ones that do not.
Adults think I am not listening. So they say the interesting things right in front of me.
I counted forty people cross this square today. I counted their pockets too. Old habit.
You want to know who came by? Ask the kid nobody looked at twice.
I remember every face that has ever shooed me off this corner. It is a long list.
Nobody tells me anything, so I just watch. Watching is free. Food, sadly, is not.
I saw the whole thing. Grown-ups never think to ask the small one in the corner.
I know every shortcut in this city. The grown-ups take the long way and call it dignity.
People whisper near me like I am furniture. I hear it all. I forget none of it.
I have stood on this corner so long the pigeons treat me as one of their own.
A kid on the street is invisible. Very handy. Less handy at dinnertime.
I notice when a stranger looks nervous. I also notice when a baker looks away.
Adults are busy being important. That is the easiest thing in the world to watch.
I could tell you who passed by all day. First, tell me why a grown-up wants to know.
I do not go to school. The street teaches faster, and never sets homework.
Everyone here is rushing somewhere important. I am going nowhere, slowly, so I see all of it.
I saw more than the guard did. He watched the gate. I watched everyone.
Give me a quiet corner and a whole day, and I will know this town better than the mayor does.
I signed eleven documents this morning. I read two of them. Do not tell the Secretary.
My whole job is paperwork about other paperwork. There is a form for the forms.
I sit below the Secretary and above the pile of files. The pile is winning.
I have a very important title and a very small desk. The desk is where I live.
I attended a meeting about scheduling meetings. I took notes. There will be a summary.
Every letter needs three stamps and two signatures. Most days I finish one letter.
I know the correct order for every document. I do not know what most of them do.
My desk has an inbox, an outbox, and a third box I am afraid to name.
I moved one file from the left pile to the right pile. That was today's achievement.
Protocol says I must be junior. I have been junior for eleven years. I am good at it.
I drafted a reply, revised the draft, then filed the revision. The reply never went out.
The Ambassador speaks. The Attache arranges. I write it all down, in triplicate.
I once found the bottom of my inbox. It was a strange and lonely afternoon.
I once requested a bigger desk. The request is still being processed. I filed it myself.
I stamped a document urgent and placed it in the pile of other urgent documents.
I am junior, so I get the forms nobody else wants. There are so many nobody wants.
I know which drawer holds which treaty. That is my entire value to this embassy.
I initialed the memo, then initialed the memo confirming I initialed the memo.
They say diplomacy is glamorous. They have not seen my filing cabinet.
By evening my hand is sore from signing. I could not name one thing I signed.
You must fill the form before we speak. Then a second form, confirming we spoke.
There is a correct way to hand someone a document. I have practiced it for years.
You used blue ink. The form requires black. I am afraid we must begin again.
Protocol is not fussy. Protocol is care, expressed through the correct number of copies.
I do not make the rules. I merely know all of them, in order, from memory.
Before you may enter, please sign here, here, and, regrettably, also here.
A missing signature is a missing bridge between two nations. I take it seriously.
I arranged the chairs by rank. It took an hour. Nobody noticed. That means I did it right.
You may skip the small talk, but you may never skip the paperwork. Never.
Everything has a proper procedure. Even, I have found, the coffee break.
I keep three pens: one to sign, one to correct, and one for emergencies of protocol.
The form must be folded precisely so. A crooked fold is a small international incident.
I do not care what you say. I care very much where you sign it.
There is an order to these things, and the order is the whole point of these things.
A guest arrived without an appointment. I offered a form to request one. He left.
Protocol says I greet you before the tea. So: greetings. Now, your documents, please.
I have a stamp for approved, a stamp for pending, and a stamp I hope never to use.
Some people find the forms tedious. I find them calming. Each box has its place.
You may think this is only a formality. It is. And formalities are my life's work.
I filed your visit correctly. Whatever happens now, the paperwork will be immaculate.
I spoke for an hour at the reception. Afterward, no one could say what about. Perfect.
My calendar is dinners, dinners, and one more dinner. I have not cooked in years.
I can say that is a wonderful question in a way that means I will not answer it.
I gave a long speech about cooperation. Halfway through, even I stopped listening.
I have a smile for hello, a smile for goodbye, and a smile for when I cannot recall your name.
I nodded, I smiled, I agreed with everyone, and I promised absolutely nothing. A good day.
The secret to diplomacy is looking fascinated by a story you have heard forty times.
I attended the dinner, praised the soup at length, and quietly avoided every real topic.
People call me a great listener. Truly, I have simply learned to nod on time.
At every reception there is a buffet, and I am the only guest too busy talking to eat.
I can turn a simple yes into a graceful, hour-long maybe. It is a delicate art.
I have cut ribbons, planted trees, and unveiled plaques. I could not tell you what any of them marked.
I shook two hundred hands tonight. I recall none of them. I smiled at each one warmly.
When two sides disagree, I speak until they forget what they disagreed about.
I once agreed with two men who disagreed with each other. Both left pleased. That is the whole skill.
At dinners I sit through speeches in three languages and applaud all of them equally.
I raised my glass to peace, to friendship, and to whatever the occasion happened to be.
I have shaken hands on agreements I did not fully understand. The photographs came out lovely.
I can discuss the weather for a full hour and make it feel like statecraft.
I nod warmly through the interpreter, then again once I hear what was actually said.
I hand out cards all night. I keep exactly none of them. It is a very generous job.
People sit down sure of themselves. They stand up humble. I mostly just make sure nobody eats the chips.
One man won everything, said thank you, and left forever. Smartest person I have ever met.
I have watched grown adults blow on dice like it changes the tiny numbers inside. It does not.
My whole job is spinning a wheel and pretending I know where it stops. I never do.
I have seen every lucky face and every unlucky face. They look the same. Just at different times.
I stand still for eight hours and move only my hands. My feet have forgotten what we do here.
A woman kissed her coins for luck before every bet. The coins remained coins. She kept kissing them.
People trust me with everyone's money and none of it is ever mine. I have stopped minding this.
I shuffle cards so much my hands do it while I sleep. My family finds this alarming.
The rule is I take no sides. So I cheer for absolutely no one, very quietly, all night long.
Someone asked me for a winning strategy. I told them the exit is that way. That is the strategy.
I have watched fortunes come and go across this little table. Mostly go. Almost always go.
I say the same three sentences all night. By closing time they have stopped meaning anything.
A boy asked if the wheel was magic. I said no, it is just very round. He was disappointed.
I hand chips out, then I gather them back. The pile is exactly the same size at dawn as at dusk.
My table has seen more tears than a sad wedding. And more hats. So many strange hats.
I never gamble myself. I have watched what happens. I go home, I make soup, I sleep fine.
People think I control the luck. I control a wheel and a small stick. That is my entire power.
A child waved at me for an hour instead of playing. Honestly the best customer I ever had.
The morning train was forty seconds late. I have not recovered, and I will not pretend I have.
I have memorized the whole timetable. Ask me anything. Please. Nobody ever asks me anything.
My job is to make trains leave on time. The trains do not always share this dream with me.
I ring the bell, I wave the little flag, the train goes. It is a small ceremony. I take it seriously.
A clock that is one minute wrong keeps me awake. I know how that sounds. I have accepted it.
People run for trains and miss them. I stand very still and catch every single one. Every day.
I have a whistle and the authority to use it. I use it exactly on schedule, never one second early.
Somebody asked when the next train comes. I told them the exact minute. They looked frightened.
The timetable is a promise. I did not write it, but I have decided to defend it with my life.
I wave goodbye to strangers all day long. None of them wave back. The trains do, sort of.
I keep this platform swept, straight, and on time. It is the tidiest thing in my entire life.
A late train is a small tragedy. A train that arrives early is somehow worse. Do not ask me why.
Thousands leave and never return. I have started taking it a little personally, which is unreasonable, I know.
I point at the big clock a lot. It is the most important object here and it agrees with me.
The rule is simple. The train leaves when I say. The train, so far, has other opinions.
I stand on this platform in every kind of weather. The trains do not thank me. I do not expect it.
A child asked to hold my flag. I said absolutely not, then let them wave it once. Just once.
Everyone here is going somewhere far. My longest journey is to the end of the platform and back, twice a day.
I check the departure board four times an hour. It never changes. I check it anyway, to be sure.
My whole day runs on minutes. When one is wasted, I feel it personally. I feel it right here.
I talk for eight hours to people I cannot see. I assume they are enjoying it. I certainly am.
My job is to fill every silence with my voice. The silence never fights back, so I always win.
I have said good morning to more strangers than anyone alive. None of them said it back.
They pay me to talk. My family finds this funny. They have been asking me to stop for years.
I read the weather, the time, and my own opinions. Only two of those are part of the job.
I sit alone in a small room and speak to thousands. It is the loneliest crowd you can imagine.
I once talked for an hour with no notes at all. Nobody stopped me. Nobody ever stops me.
My voice goes out to the whole city. My voice also does not know when to be quiet. I am working on it.
I introduce every song like it is the greatest one ever made. I have said that about all of them.
The rule is do not stop talking. I have followed this rule since I was very small. Ask my parents.
I hear my own voice all day and I have grown quite fond of it. This may be a warning sign.
A listener called to say I talk too much. I put them on air so I could respond at great length.
I say the time out loud every few minutes. It keeps me company. The clock does not talk back.
My whole job is being heard and never seen. I could be wearing anything right now. I am.
I welcome each new hour like an old friend. There are twenty-four of them. I greet them all.
Children write to ask if I ever stop talking. The honest answer is only to breathe, and barely.
I describe the whole world to people who cannot see me. Half of them are asleep. I describe it to them anyway.
I said one wrong word this morning and thought about it all day. The other ten thousand were fine.
I greet an entire city at once, out loud. The city continues about its business without comment.
A tiny light turns red and suddenly I must be interesting. It has been red for eleven years.
I run the whole show and stand where nobody can see me. This is exactly how I like it. Mostly.
The actors take their bows and their flowers. I take the quiet pride of a curtain that fell exactly on time.
I whisper into a little headset and an entire world moves. Then it stops when I say stop.
Nobody claps for me. Nobody knows my name. If I vanished, though, the lights would go out at once.
I stand in the dark all evening making sure the light finds everyone but me. That is the job.
The curtain goes up because I said so. It comes down because I said so. In between, I barely breathe.
I keep a list of everything that must happen and when. The list is longer than the show itself.
Actors forget their words and look at me. I mouth the words. I am the least seen helper alive.
My whole night is spent making sure nothing goes wrong. When nothing does, no one notices. Perfect.
I have watched this show two hundred times from the exact same dark corner. I could run it asleep.
I press a button and it snows. I press another and it stops. I am quietly in charge of the weather.
The star bows and the crowd roars. I am already three steps ahead, setting up tomorrow's roar.
I know every secret of this building. The trapdoors, the ropes, the one squeaky board. All mine.
Everyone out front thinks the magic happens on its own. It happens because I am pushing buttons very fast in the dark.
I tell grown actors when to walk and when to wait. They listen. It is the only place they ever do.
My office is a dark corner with one small light. It is not glamorous. It runs the entire evening.
When the show ends, I am the last one out. I lock the door on a room that just held a thousand people and now holds one.
A child asked who is in charge back here. I said me, very quietly, and then went back to work.
I hold the whole show in my head, cue by cue. If I sneeze at the wrong moment, chaos. So I do not.
The audience never learns my name, which is fine. If they did, something would have gone very wrong that night.
I can tell you what happened two thousand years ago exactly. Ask me what I had for lunch, though.
I began today's lecture in one century and somehow ended in another. This happens to me often.
I know the names of a hundred forgotten kings. I do not know where I left my keys. This is the trade.
A student asked what year it is. I gave them four possible answers, all from the distant past.
I love the past. It is finished, it holds still, and it never once asks me to check my messages.
My lectures have a clear beginning and, eventually, an end. What happens in the middle surprises us both.
I brought one small note to class and spoke for two hours. The note said only one word: begin.
The old days were full of drama and grand speeches. I belong in them. I was simply born a few thousand years late.
I can describe an ancient feast in delicious detail. My own kitchen remains a total mystery to me.
Students set alarms so I know when to stop. I have taught right through several of them. Gently.
I got so lost in a tangent today that I forgot the question. It was a wonderful tangent, though.
I hold the whole sweep of the ages in my head. Today's date, however, keeps slipping right out.
I told a story about a very old bridge for forty minutes. The bridge fell down long ago. I miss it.
A child asked if I was alive back then. I said no. Then I paused a very long, thoughtful while.
I could talk about a single old coin until everyone quietly leaves. Some days I test this theory.
The past is my whole world. The present keeps arriving on schedule, and I keep being politely surprised by it.
I answered a short question with a long journey through three empires. The student wanted the time.
I remember battles from a thousand years ago. I do not remember starting this sentence. Where was I.
Every fact reminds me of another fact. That is why my classes end when the building closes, not before.
I once assigned a short reading and lectured on it for a month. It was, I felt, barely enough time.
Every airport hallway looks the same and leads somewhere different. Pick one and start walking, detective.
The plane landed, your suitcase landed a little later, and your hopes landed somewhere in between.
Welcome to arrivals. Everyone here looks like they know exactly where they're going. Blend in.
You slept for six minutes on the flight and woke up ready to solve everything. Bold.
Fresh runway, fresh clues, and one foot that's been asleep since takeoff. Wake it up.
Boarding now: you, a suitcase, and a plan that fits neatly on the back of a napkin.
The seatbelt light went off, and so did your last good idea. You'll find another.
A brand-new city, and it has absolutely no idea you're here to fix everything. Surprise.
You stepped off the plane and your legs remembered how walking works about halfway down the hallway.
New skyline, new streets, new chance to walk confidently in the wrong direction.
The flight had one tiny pillow and big ideas about legroom. You survived both.
You're here! Wherever here is. Somebody wave. Nobody's waving. That's fine, you're busy.
Buckle up. The snacks are small, the flight is long, and your patience is somewhere in the overhead bin.
Another landing survived. Your knuckles can let go of the armrest now. Gently. There you go.
The doors opened and a hundred strangers all decided to leave at exactly the same moment. You among them.
You packed light, thought hard, and still can't remember which pocket you swore you put the tickets in.
Somewhere out there is a thief. Somewhere closer is a very long line for the bathroom.
You arrived a little crumpled and a lot curious. One of those will smooth out on the walk over.
You landed with a suitcase, a hunch, and the quiet confidence of someone who mostly slept.
The plane finally stopped moving, which is your body's official signal to start paying attention again.
A whole city just rolled out beneath the window. It doesn't roll back up. Might as well visit.
Boarding call. Everyone stands up at once, as if standing sooner makes the plane leave sooner. Join them.
You've arrived, gently exhausted and mostly determined. Two out of two, honestly.
Wheels down, mind up, and one earbud still in from a song that ended an hour ago.
New city, new door handles, new light switches on the wrong side. Adventure includes furniture.
The captain said we've begun our descent, and your stomach agreed, loudly and right on time.
Every trip starts the same way: with a stranger's elbow and a strong sense of purpose.
You stretched, yawned, and stepped into a city that has never once heard of your bedtime.
Solid ground at last. Your legs were folded up for hours and are still filing a formal complaint about it.
Boarding soon. You've got your bag, your notes, and one sock you're fairly sure matches.
The window seat gave you clouds, then rooftops, then this. Say hello to this.
You arrived slightly early, which means you get to stand around looking capable. Enjoy.
New time zone, new streets, and a body that firmly believes it's still yesterday.
Off the plane, down the hallway, past the shops selling things nobody needs until exactly right now.
You made it. The suitcase made it. Somewhere, a thief did not expect either of you.
The engines went quiet and the whole city got a little louder to make up for it.
You packed snacks for a two-hour flight and ate them all in the first ten minutes. Impressive, really.
New airport chairs, same impossible armrests. You'll be standing anyway. Places to be.
The trip was long, the coffee was small, and the city ahead is enormous. Fair trade.
You stepped outside, where the taxi line welcomed you with the warmth of a very long queue and no taxis.

They requested our finest room and complained it lacked the one thing it needed: more of itself.

They took the grand suite, rearranged the furniture, and left it grander than the hotel could afford.
They asked for the most expensive room and seemed disappointed we didn't have a costlier one hidden away.
They checked in under a name, complained about the towels, and checked out under quite another.
They demanded the presidential suite and asked, politely, whether we had anything above a president.

In thirty years watching this lobby I never saw a guest so proud of doing nothing wrong.
They tipped me to stop watching them, which is exactly when I started watching them.

They asked which cameras still worked, smiled at each one, and posed for it.
I follow the quiet guests. This one wanted to be followed and complained I was too slow.

They demanded the best room, refused it, then paid double for the trouble of refusing.

They asked me the fastest way out of every exit and thanked me like I had given a gift.
